summary: This topic covers the foundational elements of data communication, different modes of data transmission, various ways to arrange network devices (topologies), distinctions between local and wide area networks, and the architectural models (OSI and TCP/IP) that structure network communication.
points: Components of Data Communication: Sender, Receiver, Message, Medium, Protocol.
Duplex Modes: Simplex (one-way), Half-Duplex (two-way, alternate), Full-Duplex (two-way, simultaneous).
Network Topologies: Physical layout of a network, including Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, each with merits and demerits.
Network Types: Comparison of Local Area Network (LAN) for limited areas vs. Wide Area Network (WAN) for large geographical areas.
Network Models: OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) and TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) layered architectures and their respective layer functions.

summary: The Physical Layer is the lowest layer of the OSI model, focusing on the electrical and mechanical aspects of transmitting raw bit streams over a physical medium. Transmission media are the channels used to carry data, categorized into guided (wired) and unguided (wireless), and are subject to various impairments that affect signal quality.
points: Physical Layer Functions: Defines data rate, performs bit synchronization, decides transmission medium and physical topology (e.g., Mesh, Star, Bus, Ring), provides physical interfaces, and handles modulation.
Transmission Media: Communication channels that carry data as electromagnetic signals from sender to receiver; support Layer 1 of OSI.
Types of Media: Guided Media (e.g., copper wires, fiber optics) confine signals to a physical path; Unguided Media (e.g., air, water, vacuum) transmit signals wirelessly.
Design Factors: Bandwidth (data rate capacity), Transmission Impairment (signal degradation), and Interference (unwanted signal addition).
Transmission Impairments: Attenuation (loss of signal strength over distance), Distortion (change in signal shape), and Noise (unwanted electrical or optical energy added to the signal).

summary: The Data Link Layer (Layer 2 of OSI) ensures reliable data transfer between directly connected nodes by managing framing, flow control, error control, and medium access. It is divided into two sublayers: Logical Link Control (LLC) for error/flow control and Media Access Control (MAC) for shared medium access and addressing.
points: Data Link Layer Services: Framing (dividing data into frames), Flow Control (matching sender/receiver speeds), Error Control (detecting and correcting errors), and Medium Access Control.

Sublayers: Logical Link Control (LLC) handles communication between network layer and MAC sublayer; Media Access Control (MAC) manages access to the shared physical medium and provides unique MAC addresses.
Flow Control Mechanisms: Stop-and-Wait (sender waits for ACK after each frame) and Sliding Window (sender can transmit multiple frames before receiving ACKs).
Error Control (ARQ): Automatic Repeat Request mechanisms like Stop-and-wait ARQ and Go-Back-N ARQ use error detection, positive/negative ACKs, and retransmission for reliable delivery.

MAC Protocols (Random Access): ALOHA (Pure and Slotted), Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) with its variants (1-Persistent, Non-Persistent, P-Persistent), CSMA/CD (Collision Detection), and CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance).

IEEE 802 Project: A set of standards (e.g., 802.3 for Ethernet, 802.11 for WLAN) defining the lower two layers (Data Link and Physical) for Local Area Networks (LANs) and Metropolitan Area Networks (MANs).

summary: The Network Layer (Layer 3 of OSI) is responsible for logical addressing, routing packets across different networks (inter-networking), and determining the optimal path for data delivery from source to destination, independent of the underlying physical infrastructure.
points: Network Layer Services: Logical addressing (e.g., IP addresses), Routing (path determination), Packet forwarding (moving packets between interfaces), and Congestion control.
IPv4 Address Space: A 32-bit logical addressing scheme that provides approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses for devices on a network.

Routing Algorithms: Protocols used by routers to find the best path for data delivery, commonly categorized as Link State (each router builds a complete topology map) and Distance Vector (routers exchange routing tables with neighbors iteratively).

summary: The Transport Layer (Layer 4 of OSI) provides end-to-end communication between processes running on different hosts, ensuring reliable and ordered delivery of data. It handles segmentation, reassembly, multiplexing, and demultiplexing, offering both connection-oriented (TCP) and connectionless (UDP) services.
points: Services: Process-to-process delivery (port addressing), Segmentation and reassembly, Connection control (TCP), Flow control, Error control, and Multiplexing/Demultiplexing.
UDP (User Datagram Protocol): A connectionless, unreliable, and lightweight protocol suitable for applications where speed is more critical than guaranteed delivery (e.g., streaming, DNS).

UDP Header Analysis: A minimal header containing Source Port, Destination Port, Length, and Checksum. For example, CB84000D001C001C would have Source Port: CB84 (52100 decimal) and Destination Port: 000D (13 decimal).

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): A connection-oriented, reliable protocol providing guaranteed, ordered, and error-checked delivery of data, along with flow and congestion control. Essential for web browsing (HTTP), file transfer (FTP), and email.

summary: The Application Layer (Layer 7 of OSI) provides network services directly to end-user applications, allowing users to interact with the network. It defines specific protocols for common tasks such as file transfer, email, web browsing, and remote access, facilitating communication between different software applications.
points: Application Layer Services: Provides services like file transfer, email, remote login, web access, and network management directly to user applications.
Client-Server Model: A fundamental distributed computing model where clients request services from a server (a central resource provider), widely used across the internet.

WWW (World Wide Web) Architecture: A distributed information system built on HTTP, URLs, web servers, and web browsers, enabling global access and retrieval of hyperlinked documents and other web resources.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): The protocol for fetching resources like HTML documents. Persistent HTTP keeps the TCP connection open for multiple requests, while Non-Persistent HTTP closes the connection after each request.

Common Application Layer Protocols: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) for copying files between hosts, Email protocols (SMTP for sending, POP3/IMAP for receiving), and DNS (Domain Name System) for translating domain names to IP addresses.
